title: 2 Kings 22:1–7
context: Josiah, who walks in the ways of David, sends Shaphan in his eighteenth year to arrange repairs to the temple using the money collected from the people, entrusting it to faithful workers.

verses.text: Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jedidah the daughter of Adaiah of Bozkath.
verses.arminianNotes: Josiah begins to reign at eight and reigns thirty-one years. Arminian readers see a young king who will grow to choose faithfulness, as the following verses describe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God raising up a faithful king after two wicked reigns. Readers in this tradition note that 1 Kings 13:2 had named Josiah long before his birth.

verses.text: He did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes, and walked in all the ways of David his father, and didn’t turn away to the right hand or to the left.
verses.arminianNotes: Josiah “did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes, and walked in all the ways of David his father.” Arminian readers see wholehearted faithfulness freely pursued by the king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the highest commendation given to a king of Judah. The phrase “didn’t turn away to the right hand or to the left” describes consistent devotion to God.

verses.text: In the eighteenth year of King Josiah, the king sent Shaphan, the son of Azaliah the son of Meshullam, the scribe, to the LORD’s house, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: In his eighteenth year Josiah sends Shaphan the scribe to the LORD’s house. Arminian readers see the king taking initiative to care for the temple.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the king attending to God’s house. The precise dating marks the beginning of the events that will lead to the discovery of the book.

verses.text: “Go up to Hilkiah the high priest, that he may count the money which is brought into the LORD’s house, which the keepers of the threshold have gathered of the people.
verses.arminianNotes: He instructs, “Go up to Hilkiah the high priest, that he may count the money which is brought into the LORD’s house.” Arminian readers see orderly stewardship of the people’s offerings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see careful administration of what was given for the temple. The instructions show concern for honest use of resources.

verses.text: Let them deliver it into the hand of the workers who have the oversight of the LORD’s house; and let them give it to the workers who are in the LORD’s house, to repair the damage to the house,
verses.arminianNotes: The money is to go to the workers “to repair the damage to the house.” Arminian readers see the restoration of worship beginning with practical repair of the sanctuary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see attention to the physical house of God. The repair work provides the setting for the discovery of the book of the law.

verses.text: to the carpenters, and to the builders, and to the masons, and for buying timber and cut stone to repair the house.
verses.arminianNotes: The money goes to carpenters, builders, masons, and for timber and stone. Arminian readers see ordinary labor dedicated to God’s house, valued as service to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the practical details of restoration. The list of workers and materials grounds the account in the concrete work of repairing the temple.

verses.text: However, no accounting shall be asked of them for the money delivered into their hand, for they deal faithfully.”
verses.arminianNotes: “… no accounting shall be asked of them for the money delivered into their hand, for they deal faithfully.” Arminian readers see trust placed in honest workers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see faithfulness in the workers commended. The note reflects a community in which integrity marked those serving God’s house.
